title: Investigation Station
strapline: Magnifiers, magnets and a table full of 'I wonder' — where questions get taken seriously and tested properly.
intent: Children learn the investigator's loop: wonder, predict, test, look closely, say what happened.
Children examine the real world in detail — magnified feathers, snail trails, seed heads, rust — and find that ordinary things get stranger the closer you look.
Children sort and classify by evidence: magnetic or not, floats or sinks, dissolves or doesn't.
Children handle scientific tools properly — magnifiers, pipettes, tweezers, magnets, balance scales — and learn each tool's job.
Children treat every living visitor to the table with gentleness: observed, wondered at, and returned where it was found.
Children build the language of finding out: predict, test, compare, because, what if.
implementation: Refresh the table with a genuine mystery, not a display — one strange object (a whole nutmeg, a bird's nest fallen after a storm, a rusty key) beats ten labelled ones.
Answer questions with investigations: 'I don't know — how could we find out?' is the house style here.
Ask for the prediction first and write it down in front of the child — then test, then come back to what they said.
Show the proper use of each tool once, briefly — pipette squeeze-and-release, magnifier close to the eye — then hand it over for keeps.
Set up sorting tests with two labelled trays — magnetic/not magnetic, floats/sinks — and let children run the whole trial and re-sort the surprises.
Establish the living-things rule from day one: we look, we're gentle, we put it back — and model it with every woodlouse.
Keep a floorbook of the station's questions, predictions, photos and findings, and read it back — children love meeting their own old theories.
key_questions: What do you notice that you couldn't see before?
What do you think will happen — and what makes you think that?
Is that what you expected? What surprised you?
Where should we put it back — and why there?

impact.text: Children explore how mechanisms work — old locks and keys, hinges, egg whisks, wind-up toys — turning and testing until they get it.
Children bring treasures from walks and the garden to the station and talk about what they've found.
Children ask real questions at the table and expect real answers — or better, a way to find out.
Children run tests of floating, sinking, dissolving and mixing, and describe the change they see.
Children make a prediction, test it and compare the result with what they said — 'I thought it would sink but it floated!'
Children sort objects by what the test showed — magnetic and not, floaters and sinkers — noticing same and different.
Children handle snails, worms and woodlice visitors gently and return them where they were found, without being told.
Children use pipettes, tweezers and droppers with precision and patience during their investigations.

enhancements: A mystery object of the week under a cloth — feel first, guess, then reveal and investigate.
A magnet hunt: one strong magnet, one bucket, the whole room — then sort the haul and hunt the surprises.
Melting watch: an ice balloon on a tray with salt, pipettes of warm water and a timer.
A snail visitor for the morning — magnifiers, a lettuce leaf, silvery trail on black paper, then home to the garden.
A smells bar: numbered jars of coffee, lemon, mint and vinegar to sniff, guess and match to photos.
Take-apart Tuesday: an old (cable-less, battery-free) clock or keyboard, real screwdrivers, and permission to see inside.
Rust farm: nails in jars — dry, water, salty water — checked and photographed across the month.

playing_exploring: A strange object and a magnifier is all the invitation most children need — curiosity does the rest.
Children poke, turn, sniff and test on their own terms before any adult framing arrives.
active_learning: Investigations run across days — the rust jars and the floorbook keep children returning to check.
Being surprised by a result, and wanting to know why, powers the next test.
creating_thinking: Children form theories, test them and change their minds in the face of evidence — the whole scientific method, pocket-sized.
They link findings across investigations: 'metal sank AND it stuck to the magnet'.
